full_judgment:
SK Sinha J: Informant Md Ziaul Huq Chowdhury obtained this Rule against the order dated 7-6-03 of the Additional Sessions Judge, 3rd Court, Chittagong in Sessions Trial Case No. 1 of 2001 discharging the opposite party No.2 Mofizur Rahman alias Mofizul Azam on the ground that there is no sufficient evidence to proceed against him. Since the petitioner has annexed the statements of all the witnesses recorded under section 161 CrPC along with the first information report, the police report, the record of the case at this late stage is not necessary, the application for calling for the record is accordingly rejected. 

 2. Facts relevant for the disposal of the Rule are as follows: Petitioner lodged a first information report with the Banskhali police station on 21-3-99 against Mofizur Rahman and four other accused persons alleging, inter alia, that the accused persons demanded toll of Taka 20,000 on 17-3-99 from the victim Enamul Huq Chowdhury; the father of the informant, and as he did not satisfy their demand they attacked him, and as per order of Mofizur Rahman, the other accused persons assaulted him mercilessly causing severe injuries rand thereafter, Mofizur Rahman snatched away Taka 4,000 from his pocket. Victim died at Chittagong Medical College Hospital. Pursuant to the first information report, the police registered a case and after investigation submitted a report in favour of Mofizur Rahman recommending for his discharge and charge-sheet against other four accused. Petitioner filed a naraji petition against the submission of the final report. The learned Magistrate rejected the final report submitted in favour of Mofizur Rahman and took cognisance of the offence under sections 304/379/34 of the Penal Code against all the first information report named accused persons by order dated 25-5-2000. The case record was eventually sent to the learned Sessions Judge for trial. Before the Additional Sessions Judge, 3rd Court, Chittagong who received the case record for trial, Mofizur Rahman filed an application for discharge under section 265C of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The learned Additional Sessions Judge allowed the application and discharged him on the reasoning that there is no sufficient material on record to frame charge against him. The learned Additional Sessions Judge, however, framed charge against other four accused persons under sections 304/379/34 of the Penal Code by the impugned order dated 7-6-2003. 

 4. Mr Mujibur Rahman, learned Advocate, on the other hand, submits that after deletion of Chapter XVIII by the Law Reform Ordinance No. XLIX of 1978 with effect from 1st June, 1979, a Magistrate having power to take cognisance of an offence has no power to take cognisance of an offence in respect of a case which is exclusively triable by a Court of Session on the basis of a naraji petition. According to him, in respect of such cases, the Magistrate has no alternative but to send the record of the case to the Court of Sessions for passing appropriate order under section 205C. His second contention is that after repeal of chapter XVIII of the Code, a duty is cast upon the Court of Session at the time of framing charge against an accused person to examine the record of the case for ascertaining whether or not there is sufficient material for presuming that the accused has committed an offence and that the Court has no power to pass any order mechanically. His further contention is that if a superior police officer is appointed to supervise the case, no investigating officer has any power to exercise his discretion to file a police report in either way without the permission of the said superior police officer, and since in this particular case a superior officer has been appointed, the investigating officer has acted as per direction of the superior officer for submitting final report in favour of Mofizur Rahman. He finally submits that no fruitful purpose will be served if accused Mofizur Rahman is put on trial, inasmuch as, all but one witness have stated that Mofizur Rahman has been found standing nearer to the place of occurrence without attributing any overt act of actively participating in the incident against him. According to him, mere presence of Mofizur Rahman does not infer the existence of a common intention animating to doing a criminal act in furtherance of common intention and in support of his contention, he has referred some decisions, the cases of Amar Kumar Thakur and others vs State 1988 BLD (AD) 101 = 40 DLR (AD) 147, Hajee Md Ahsanullah vs Arafatunnessa Bibi being dead his heirs Ali Ahmed and others, 33 DLR (AD)17, Rangaswami vs State of Tamil Nadu AIR 1989 (SC) 1137 and Rambilas Singh and others vs State of Bihar, AIR 1989 (SC) 1593. 

 5. Before we decide the legal points, let us consider whether or not there is sufficient ground for proceeding against accused Mofizur Rahman or that the learned Additional Sessions Judge has rightly discharged him. Accused Mofizur Rahman has been arrayed as accused serial No. 1 in the first information report. There is allegation against him that as per his order, other accused persons have mercilessly assaulted the victim and that he has snatched away Taka 4,000 from the pocket of the victim. In the naraji petition the petitioner has alleged that Mofizur Rahman is the principal accused at whose instance the incident has taken place, that the investigating officer has inserted a statement of the victim under section 161, CrPC in the case diary which is not the true version of the victim and that although witnesses No. 2-8, 15, 17-19 have stated about the active participation of accused Mofizur Rahman in corroborating with the first information report version, he has recorded their statements evasively excluding the incriminating portions relating to Mofizur Rahman's participation in the occurrence. The learned Magistrate performed formalities after receipt of the naraji petition, and called for the case diary, heard the learned Advocates at length and on perusal of the case diary noticed that two police officers had investigated the case, that despite the change of the investigating officer, the case diary was written by one officer which was unusual, that Sub-Inspector' Habibur Rahman recorded statement of Afsarul Huq on 22-3-99 who stated that as per order of Mofizur Rahman the incident took place, that opposite to page 92 of the diary there was noting that he examined the victim in the Chittagong Medical College Hospital on 4-5-99 in presence of the witnesses but the victim died on 20-4-99, that the investigating officer having found the complicity of Mofizur Rahman submitted the memo of evidence to his higher authority seeking permission to submit charge-sheet against all the accused persons, that in the memo of evidence the investigating officer observed that Mofizur Rahman had dispute with the deceased over 4 decimals of land and that as per his order the occurrence took place. The learned Magistrate after consideration of the case diary meticulously by a reasoned order rejected the recommendation of the investigating officer and took cognisance of the offence against accused Mofizur Rahman. 

 6. On perusal of the statements of the witnesses recorded under section 161, CrPC, we noticed that the investigating officers had examined 17 witnesses, of them, Ashraful Huq's statement was recorded on 22-3-99, the statements of five witnesses were recorded on 10-5-99, six of them were examined on 17-5-99, three of them were on two dates in June, 1999 and two of them were on 7-8-99. Only the victim's statement was recorded on 4-5-99. We failed to understand why the investigating officer did not arrange for recording the victim's dying declaration during this period and opted to record his statement under section 161. After examination of one witness, there was a long gap in recording statements of the witnesses and even after examination of the victim, he killed time and then started recording the statements of the witnesses. The learned Magistrate noticed the writing in the diary by the same officer despite the change of the investigating officer, and different handwriting and the signature of the officer in the statement of the victim, although the officer who recorded the statement was required to give his signature. In view of the above, he suspected something unusual in the conduct of the investigating officer of the case. In view of the above, he found substance of the informant's claim that the investigating officer was not impartial who on being influenced by Mofizur Rahman had submitted the report in his favour. He observed that initially the investigating officer had found prima facie complicity of Mofizur Rahman and sought permission to submit charge-sheet against him in the memo of evidence but subsequently, he had changed his motive. With such observations, he has rejected the investigating officer's recommendation and after perusal of the case diary minutely, came to the conclusion that there is sufficient material on record for taking cognisance of offence against Mofizur Rahman. 

 7. The learned Additional Sessions Judge made inconsistent observations while discharging accused Mofizur Rahman. He observed "it does not appear from the order of the learned Magistrate that on considering which paper available on record, he incorporated the name of the accused Mofizur Rahman in the charge-sheet whose name has not been sent up in the charge-sheet, as the investigating officer has found nothing against him in the investigation. Now I am of the opinion that before incorporating accused Mofizur Rahman in the charge-sheet though the investigating officer found nothing against him, the learned Magistrate ought to have considered the papers on record". The question is, whether in the facts of the given case the learned Magistrate is justified in taking cognisance of the offence against Mofizur Rahman on rejecting the police recommendation. The question of inclusion of the name of Mofizur Rahman in the charge-sheet by a Magistrate while taking cognisance of the offence on the basis of the police report does not arise. The observation that accused Mofizur Rahman's name was inserted in the charge-sheet by the Magistrate, even though the investigating officer did not find prima facie case against him, is misconceived one, inasmuch as the learned Magistrate took cognisance of the offence on the basis of the case diary and the naraji petition. A naraji petmon is a complaint for all practical purposes and if a Magistrate having power to take cognisance of the offence is satisfied on examination of the complainant that the complaint discloses an offence he can take cognisance of the offence, against the accused under section 190(1)(b), irrespective of an offence which is exclusively triable by a Court of Session. 

 8. If a police officer submits a final report in favour of an accused in a case, a Magistrate having power to take cognisance of any offence has two alternatives; he can send the case to the police for further investigation if he does not agree with the police report, or in the alternative, he may take cognisance of the offence on rejecting the investigating officer's recommendation on perusal of the case diary, if he findsprima Jaciecase against him. Normally, a Magistrate does not resort to the painstaking task of perusing the case diary if there is recommendation for the discharge of an accused but in this particular case, the learned Magistrate has resorted to the latter option. This is the absolute discretionary power of the Magistrate. The words "report in writing of such facts made by a police officer" in clause (b) of section 190(1) would include a report by the police in any case they can investigate under chapter XIV The police report includes not only the final report under section 173 but also other reports made by the police. The report is not binding on the Magistrate and the Magistrate, notwithstanding the recommendation of the investigating officer to discharge the accused and proceed to take cognisance and summon the accused to face trial. The observation of learned Additional Sessions Judge that witness Ashraful Huq out of emotion made allegation against accused Mofizur Rahman is based upon non-application of judicial mind in that besides. Ashraful Huq, the informant also made specific allegations against Mofizur Rahman in the first information report and in the naraji petition, Secondly, even if it is assumed that victim Enamul Huq Chowdhury has made a statement under section 161 before the investigating officer. in the manner he has recorded, such statement cannot be used for any purpose at the trial other than for contradicting him, which is not possible, as he has succumbed to the injuries. If we treat this statement as dying declaration it is difficult to use the same as such since the informant has disputed the correctness of the statement of the maker stating that the investigating officer has recorded his statement at his whim. The learned 'Additional Sessions Judge has failed to consider that aspect of the matter and illegally stresses upon the statement of the victim and the recommendation of the investigating officer in failing to notice that a naraji petition in a case is filed when the informant or complainant is dissatisfied with the conduct of the investigating officer in not properly investigating the case. 

 9. Section 265C empowers a Court to discharge an accused if it considers that there is no sufficient ground for proceeding against such accused. The Court is required to consider the record of the case and the documents submitted therewith and to record reason if it considers that there is no sufficient ground for proceeding against the accused. A first information report or a complaint is a part of the record of the case and both in the first information report and the complaint; there are specific allegations against the accused Mofizur Rahman of taking active role in the occurrence. Some other witnesses stated that he was found standing adjacent to place of occurrence. In his naraji petition there is allegation that. the investigating officer has recorded the statements of those witnesses at his whim and not according to the version of those witnesses. The learned Additional Sessions Judge instead of forming his opinion on the basis of the case diary and the naraji petition has stressed upon the observations of the police officer in failing to notice that the informant has challenged the police report stating that the investigating officer has not properly recorded the statements of the victim and other witnesses. Since the learned Magistrate on perusal of the case diary and the complaint was satisfied that the investigating officer did not properly investigate the case, the learned Additional Sessions Judge should have come to a definite finding as to the correctness of the observations of the learned Magistrate on perusal of the materials on record. In the facts of the given case, we are of the view the learned Magistrate is justified in taking cognisance of offence against accused Mofizur Rahman. We find merit in the contention of the learned Advocate for the petitioner that the learned Additional Sessions Judge has committed error of law in discharging Mofizur Rahman. 

 10. Let us now turn to the legal aspects of the case. Chapter XXIII, in which, section 265C contains, has been substituted for the original Chapter XXIII by Ordinance No. XLIX of 1978. This chapter came into force with effect from 1st June, 1979. In the old chapter XXIII, there was a provision for discharge of an accused under section 209 CrPC, which is almost in the verbatim language of section 265C, which are as follows: 

 "209 When the evidence referred to in section 208, sub-sections (1) and (3) has been taken, and he has (if necessary) examined the accused such Magistrate shall, if he finds that there are not sufficient grounds for committing the accused person for trial, record his reasons and discharge him, unless it appears to the Magistrate that such person should be tried before himself or some other Magistrate in which case, he shall proceed accordingly. 

 "265C. If upon consideration of the record of the case and the documents submitted therewith, and after hearing the submissions of the accused and the prosecution in this behalf, the Court considers that there is no sufficient ground for proceeding against the accused, it shall discharge the accused and record the reasons for so doing". 

 11. The words "evidence referred to in section 208" have been used in section 209 and in its place the words "the record of the case and the documents submitted therewith" have been used in section 205C. Section 209 contemplates an order of discharge by a Magistrate during the inquiry into an  offence triable by a Court of Session, if the evidence establishes that there are not sufficient grounds for committing the accused, whereas, in new provision this power of discharge has been given to a Court of Session who on consideration of the record and the documents submitted therewith i.e., the first information report, statements of the witnesses, the other documents, such as, the seizure list, inquest report and post mortem report, if there be any, and such other documents if seized in course of the investigation of the case but not the documents to be submitted by the accused person in support of his prayer for discharge, may make an order of discharge if it considers that there is no ground for proceeding against the accused. In the Indian Code of 1973, the procedure for' commitment enquiry in respect of cases exclusively triable by a Court of Session has been dispensed with and a Magistrate is empowered to perform certain preliminary function under section 209 before sending the case record for trial, which reads as follows: 

 "209. Commitment of case to the Court of Session when offence is triable exclusively by it. When in a case instituted on a police report or otherwise, the accused appears or is brought before the Magistrate and it appears to the Magistrate that the offence is triable exclusively by the Court of Session, he shall commit, after complying with the provisions of section 207 or section 208, as the case may be, the case to the Court of Session, and subject to the provisions of this Code relating to bail, remand the accused to custody until such commitment has been made. 

 (b) subject to the provisions of this Code relating to bail, remand the accused to custody during, and until the conclusion of the trial, (c) send.to that Court the record of the case and the documents and articles, if any, which are to be produced in evidence. 

 (d) notify the Public Prosecutor of the commitment of the case to the Court of Session." 

 12. The Law Commission of India while recommending to insert this provision in the Code observed, the preliminary enquiry prescribed under the old Code served no useful purpose and on the contrary involved a great deal of infructuous work causing delay in the trial of serious cases and that provision is made in the new section for performing certain preliminary functions like granting copies, preparing the record, notifying the public prosecutor, etc. It was further observed "It will be convenient to refer to this process as commitment of the case to the Court of Session although the procedure is radically different from the commitment proceedings at present provided in chapter 18" 

 Transfer of case of Court of Session when offence is triable exclusively by it. 

 "2-C-When in a case instituted on a police report or otherwise, the accused appears or is brought before the Magistrate and it appears to the Magistrate that the offence is triable exclusively by the Court of Session, he shall 

 a) send the case to the Court of Session; 

 c) send to that Court the record of the case and the documents and articles, if any, which are to be produced in evidence. 

 d) notify the Public Prosecutor of the transfer of the case to the Court of Session." 

 14. The difference between the two provisions is that under the Indian Provision, in place of expressions "commitment of case to Court of session when the offence is triable exclusively by it" used to the prefix of the section, the expressions "transfer of case of Court of Session when the offence is triable exclusively by it." have been used in the marginal note. In clause (a) of section 209. the word "commit" has been used, whereas the word "send" in clause (a) of section 205 has been used. Section 205C has been placed in Chapter XVII Under the heading" OF THE COMMENCEMENT OF PROCEEDINGS BEFORE MAGISTRATE." This chapter starts with section 204 empowering a Magistrate taking cognisance of an offence to issue process if he finds sufficient ground for proceeding against an accused. This is the only section authorising a Magistrate to issue process to an accused after taking cognisance of an offence either on complaint or on police report or upon his own knowledge. Unless the Magistrate takes cognisance of an offence under section 190, a process cannot be issued under section 204. Section 205 empowers such Magistrate to dispense with the personal attendance of an accused. Section 205C as mentioned above, is followed by section 205CC empowering such Magistrate to transfer a case to the District Magistrate in respect of offences exclusively triable by a District or an Additional District Magistrate. Section 190 empowers Magistrates specified therein to take cognisance of any offence under three eventualities as mentioned above. 

 15. Section 193 provides that except otherwise expressly provided by the Code or by any other law for the time being in force, no Court of Session shall take cognisance of any offence as a Court of original jurisdiction unless the accused has been sent to it by a Magistrate duly empowered in that behalf. Similar provision in section 193 is provided in the Indian Code of 1973. Section 193(1) lays down that a Court of Session is not a Court of original jurisdiction but it may seize a case only when a Magistrate sends the case. It cannot entertain any direct complaint or pass any order thereon unless a Magistrate forwards the same to it. The conspectus of sections 190, 193, 204 and 205C clearly suggests that the powers for taking cognisance of an offence and issuance of a process either in respect of a case triable by a Magistrate or by a Court of Session have been given to the specified Magistrates and a Court of Session has no power in that regard as a Court of original jurisdiction and unless the case is sent for trial, it has no power to hold trial of the case. The powers of such Magistrates and that of a Court of Session are defined in the Code. This power and jurisdiction of a Magistrate has not been affected even after the abolition of Chapter XVIII. In view of the above, we find fallacy in the contention of Md Mujibur Rahman that a Magistrate has no power to accept a naraji petition and to take cognisance of an offence in respect of a case exclusively triable by a Court of Session if a final report is filed in favour of an accused. 

 16. In the case of Abdus Salam Master alias Salam and another vs State, 36 DLR (AD) 58, one Kallyan Behari Das succumbed to injury and over the said incident a first information report was lodged. The police after investigation submitted a final report in favour of the accused. The Magistrate accepted the final report. A fresh complaint was filed making similar allegation. The Magistrate after holding an inquiry took cognisance of the offence. Accused Abdus Salam being unsuccessful before the High Court Division for quashing the proceedings, moved a leave petition before the Appellate Division. The Appellate Division observed: "The Magistrate, however, is not bound to accept the recommendation made by the Investigating Officer in his report but he is required to apply his judicial discretion and he may disagree with the Investigating Officer. If the recommendation is that the accused should be discharged, in other words, if final report has been submitted, the Magistrate may, on rejecting recommendation adopt either of the two courses." In that case of Shamsun Nahar alias Maina vs State, 1984 BLD (AD) 206, the police submitted a final report in favour of an accused and charge-sheet against another. The Magistrate accepted the police report and discharged the accused in whose favour final report was submitted. Thereafter, the Magistrate sent back the case for further investigation to the police, asking investigating officer to submit charge-sheet under proper section against the said accused. The Appellate Division was of the view that once a Magistrate has taken cognisance on a police report, he is not entitled to send the case to the police for further investigation. The Appellate Division observed: "If, however, he is not satisfied with the final report, he is competent when he receives the police report to take cognisance against the accused in favour of whom final report was submitted under the provisions of Section 190(b) of the Code of Criminal Procedure." In the case of Abdur Rahman vs State, 29 DLR (SC) 256 it was observed: "Rule 276(b) of the Police Regulation provides that the Magistrate may accept the final report or direct further enquiry under section 156(b) of the Code, or he may take cognisance under section 190(1 )(b) of the Code." 

 17. In the case of Bangladesh vs Yakub Sardar and others 40 DLR (AD) 246, the facts are as follows: one Monsur Sardar was murdered and over the said incident a relation of the deceased lodged a first information report which gave rise to Sessions Case No. 51 of 1981. After ten days of murder, Monsur's son made a complaint against another set of accused. The learned Magistrate sent the complaint to the police for inquiry. On a criminal motion moved against that order, the learned Sessions Judge directed the Magistrate to follow section 205D. Thereafter, on the prayer of the complainant to withdraw the complaint, the learned Magistrate dismissed the complaint. A nephew of the deceased, who was cited as witness Amir Khan, moved another criminal motion against the order of the learned Magistrate dismissing the complaint. The learned Sessions Judge directed the Magistrate to hold further inquiry into the matter. The Magistrate on holding inquiry dismissed the complaint under section 203. This dismissal order was again challenged in a revision petition. The learned Sessions Judge directed the Magistrate to send the complaint case treating the case as counter- case of Sessions Case No. 51 of 1981. The High Court Division quashed this order of the Sessions Judge. As the learned Magistrate did not issue any process on the basis of the complaint, the Appellate Division granted leave to consider whether a "Sessions Judge has got power to direct the Magistrate to send the case to him" for trial. The Appellate Division found the order of the High Court Division was not proper and observed that the "proper course for the High Court Division was to modify the Session's Judge's order and to direct further inquiry under section 436." It is thus clear from the above cases that a Court of Session has no power to take cognisance of any offence as a Court of original jurisdiction and that the Magistrate having power to take cognisance of any offence has exclusive power to take cognisance of an offence and to issue process irrespective of any offence, either he has power to hold trial of the case or not. In view of these consistent views, we find no substance in the contention of the learned Advocate for the opposite party. 

 18. Mr Mujibur Rahman submits that, since the investigating officer has submitted final report in favour of Mofizur Rahman as per direction of superior officer, he has no option other than to obey the direction of his superior officer and thereby he has made no illegality in submitting such report. This is a confused submission. A police report submitted by a police officer after investigation of a case in exercise of powers under Chapter XIV itself is not a proof of guilt or innocence of accused and it is for the Court to adjudicate upon it, and come to its own conclusion on evidence to be produced as to whether any offence is made out or not. When a police officer has not conducted the investigation properly and in accordance with law, the Magistrate has power to direct investigation by any other police officer or agency. A superior police officer may direct the officer-in charge of a police station to make further investigation pending orders of the Magistrate under sub-section (2) of section 173 in respect of reports to be submitted under section 158. Section 158 relates to a police report in respect of an investigation of a case conducted under section 157 where the commission of a cognisable offence is suspected and such report be submitted through a superior officer of police as may be appointed. A police officer is under statutory duty to investigate into commission of a cognisable offence on the basis of a report having been made to that effect, and in such cases, no superior officer is required to be appointed. In this case the investigation was started under section 156(1) on the basis of a first information report lodged by the petitioner, which disclosed a cognisable offence. We find no merit in his contention. 

 19. As regards the contention of the learned Advocate that mere presence of Mofizur Rahman near the place of occurrence does not attract section 34 of the Penal Code. We are of the view that this is not the appropriate stage to decide whether or not accused Mofizur Rahman has common intention to commit the offence. The essence of liability under section 34 is to be found in the existence of a common intention animating the offenders leading to the doing of a criminal act in furtherance of the common intention and presence of the offender sought to be rendered liable which will be decided on the assessment of the evidence. We do not dispute the proposition of law stated in those cases referred by Mr. Rahman but those cases are not applicable in this case. We have noticed that the learned Additional Sessions Judge has framed charge under sections 304/379/34 of the Penal Code in a lump against all four accused persons. Section 304 prescribes the sentence for the offence of culpable homicide not amounting to murder, the sentence varying according to offender's intention or knowledge. The learned Additional Sessions Judge is required to mention under which part of section 304 the accused persons are facing trial but he has not clarified that aspect. There is allegation against Mofizur Rahman and Touhidul Islam of snatching away money. There is no allegation against other accused persons in that regard but he has framed charge under section 379 against all the four accused persons. In that view of the matter, we find that the learned Additional Sessions Judge has not applied his judicial mind in framing charge against the accused persons. Accused Mofizur Rahman was discharged at a stage after his complicity was found by the Magistrate and taking cognisance of the offence against him, and, as such, no formal inquiry under section 436 is required to be taken for ascertaining his complicity in the case. Accordingly, we direct the learned Additional Sessions Judge to frame charge afresh on consideration of the materials on record and in the light of the observations made above. We find merit in this Rule. 

 In the result, the Rule is made absolute. The impugned order is set aside. The learned Additional Sessions Judge is directed to proceed with the case in the light of the observations made above.
